sentences.text: Hello, everyone.
I am Dr. Cesar Marolla, Instructor at Harvard University Division of Continuing Education.
I developed the Risk Mechanism Theory Index, RMTI, to turn what we can measure into one score that I can follow over time.
Here I apply it to breast cancer.
I start with a published case study: O'Shaughnessy and colleagues, Breast Cancer Research and Treatment, 2026.
Among 5,041 women with metastatic hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer, survival after first post-endocrine chemotherapy was 13.5 months, and 30 percent died before a second-line regimen.
I follow the tumor through four stages.
Stage one: a small invasive tumor, with lymph nodes clear or minimally involved.
Stage two: a larger tumor, or involvement of axillary lymph nodes.
Stage three: extensive nodal disease, or spread to the chest wall or skin.
Stage four: distant metastasis, for example to bone or liver.
Now I assess the data.
I use prior CDK 4/6 inhibitor use for likelihood; performance status and metastatic burden for vulnerability; and the 30 percent who die before second line for resilience.
This mapping is illustrative.
Then I calculate.
R equals L times E times V times one minus rho.
With these illustrative inputs, R is 0.054, band two of the fixed five-band scale.
Expected Annual Loss adds consequences.
I follow the trajectory.
At each review cycle I update vulnerability and resilience.
In this synthetic example, as I close the delivery gap, R falls from 0.054 to 0.023, band two to band one.
It is an illustration, not a prediction.
With RMTI, I quantify risk as one score, assess it on fixed bands, and track vulnerability and resilience across cycles.
Treatment decisions stay with clinicians.
RMTI is a research prototype: uncalibrated, with synthetic examples, and not a medical device.
I am testing whether trajectory adds information beyond the current level.
Thank you for watching.
